title: Elara’s Orchard: Blight and Branching Choices

scenario.title: Elara’s Orchard: Blight and Branching Choices
scenario.setting: Elara’s Orchard is divided into 12 interconnected microcells: heirloom apple guild beds, mason bee nesting boxes, rain-harvest cisterns, and stone fruit barrier rows. Planted by their great-grandmother 13 years prior, it’s now sustained by three sibling stewards and a rotating crew of local volunteers, having cleared its first critical growth year and entered its second decade of production. The core dilemma hinges on the orchard’s original cider apple tree, whose root flare shows signs of neonatal blight, splitting the siblings over how best to save it.

characters.name: Mara
characters.tendencies: She curates the siblings' shared digital archive of great-grandma's orchard notes, cross-referencing weekly microcell surveys against Elara’s original planting plan. She refuses to consider untested treatments because she fears losing the orchard's original ancestral lineage.

characters.name: Lila
characters.tendencies: She’s spent the last three months trialing organic copper sulfate sprays on the affected tree, refining application rates to minimize harm to nearby pollinator habitats. She argues that delaying the experimental treatment will lead to the tree's death before the autumn harvest.

characters.name: Javi
characters.tendencies: He runs the orchard’s community-supported agriculture program, hosting monthly open houses and recruiting local volunteers to assist with daily maintenance. He worries that diverting all their resources to saving one tree will leave other parts of the orchard’s microcell network under-cared for.

characters.name: Kaelin
characters.tendencies: They’re a local teen volunteer who first discovered the orchard through Javi’s social media posts, and they’ve begun documenting the orchard’s unplanned volunteer saplings. They’ve noticed new shoots sprouting from the base of the blighted tree, and they advocate for letting natural regeneration lead the way.

turns.name: DM
turns.text: Salt fog rolls off the harbor as the tide-bells ring dusk, and you

turns.name: Mara
turns.text:
I’m hunched over my waterproof tablet, cross-referencing Microcell 7’s heirloom apple guild survey against Elara’s handwritten 1997 planting log. The salt fog is glitching my satellite tracker, so I’m manually verifying each bed’s GPS coordinates to make sure I don’t misfile this week’s data against the wrong ancestral planting plan.
[tucks a crinkled printed microcell survey sheet back into the water-resistant leather binder strapped to her hip]

turns.name: Javi
turns.text:
Between rushing to shore up that ailing heritage apple tree and prepping for tonight’s CSA open house, half our volunteer crew is already tied up elsewhere. I can’t shake the gnawing worry we’re letting too many of the smaller microcell plots—from mason bee box cleanups to cistern top-offs—slip through the cracks right now.
[drops the stack of open house cookie platters he’s carrying onto a splintered wooden crate, then runs a hand through his sun-bleached hair]

turns.name: Kaelin
turns.text:
Look at these delicate new shoots sprouting from the base of that blighted apple tree! We should hold off on removing it entirely and let this natural regeneration take root instead of rushing to plant a store-bought sapling. The tide bells just rang, too—perfect timing to jot this observation down before dusk fades.
[kneels in the damp clover at the tree’s base, unclipping their frayed ballpoint pen from their tattered field notebook to sketch the tiny new saplings]

turns.name: Mara
turns.text:
I tap the fog-glitched satellite tracker on my waterproof tablet with a sharp sigh, then gesture at the new basal shoots sprouting at the blighted tree’s base. Elara’s 1997 planting log for Microcell 7 strictly bars allowing unvetted regrowth, as it could dilute the direct ancestral lineage of this heirloom apple cultivar. We need to trim these shoots back with our approved organic pruning protocol instead of letting them take root.
[steps closer to the blighted apple tree to make precise, targeted cuts on the tender new basal shoots]

turns.name: Lila
turns.text: Kaelin, those shoots are just sucker growth from the rootstock—they'll never ripen fruit worth saving, and every week we debate is a week the canker spreads deeper into the heartwood. I've spent three months dialing these copper rates down precisely so the spray won't drift into the mason bee boxes, and I can show you the application logs right now if you want proof. If we wait past this fog season, we'll be harvesting deadwood instead of apples come autumn. [pulls her field notebook from her coat pocket and flips it open to the spray schedule, holding it out toward Kaelin]

turns.name: Javi
turns.text: That’s a thoughtful call, but we can’t let the rest of the orchard’s microcells fall by the wayside while we focus on this single apple tree. The mason bee nesting boxes in Microcell 2 need a full tidy before dusk, and tonight’s CSA open house attendees will be touring the rain cisterns at Microcell 9, which haven’t been prepped yet. Let’s circle back to this tree’s future once we’ve knocked those priority tasks off our list. [grabs a stack of volunteer checklists and a spray bottle of disinfectant from his nearby tool caddy]

turns.name: Kaelin
turns.text:
I swipe to pull up my detailed field notes on this tree’s root sprouts, gesturing toward the tiny green growths at its base. These natural saplings are perfectly adapted to this orchard’s salt fog and coastal soil, so letting them take root makes far more sense than felling the whole mature tree.
[kneels to brush back a thick mat of dead grass obscuring more of the hidden tender shoots]
